{"candidate_slot":1,"current_prompt":"You are given a JSON object with two top-level keys: 'system_profile' (an inventory of installed software/components, including product names, versions, and identifying details) and 'advisories' (a list of CVE advisories, each with an ID, description, and affected-product/version information). Determine which of the SUPPLIED advisories apply to the INSTALLED system, and return their IDs.

PROCEDURE:

1. BUILD A FULL INDEX OF THE SYSTEM PROFILE FIRST. Record every installed product, its exact version string, and context (OS, architecture, edition, packaging, vendor). CRITICALLY, also index every sub-component, bundled dependency, library, runtime, and nested entry anywhere in the profile — inside package manifests, dependency lists, requirements files, container layers, or embedded within other products. If a component is explicitly listed as installed, even as a dependency of something else, it counts as installed. Most matching errors come from failing to index these nested components, so be exhaustive here before evaluating any advisory.

2. MATCH PRODUCTS FLEXIBLY BUT CORRECTLY. An advisory is a candidate only if it concerns a product genuinely present in the profile. Compare product names precisely, treating clear variants and aliases as equivalent: 'OpenSSL' = 'openssl'; 'Apache HTTP Server' = 'httpd' = 'apache2'; vendor prefixes may differ ('Red Hat Enterprise Linux' vs 'RHEL'); package-name decorations ('lib', '-dev', '-devel', ecosystem names like pip/npm/gem/deb/rpm package identifiers vs upstream project names) do not change identity. An advisory for a LIBRARY applies if that library is installed, regardless of which application bundles it. However, reject different products that merely share a word: 'nginx-ingress-controller' is not plain 'nginx'; 'log4j' is not 'log4net'. Distinguish libraries from applications and server from client components of the same family when the advisory is specific.

3. EVALUATE VERSION INFORMATION CAREFULLY. Once the product matches, compare the installed version against the advisory's affected version information using its stated semantics exactly: '< 1.2.3' or 'up to, excluding 1.2.3' means 1.2.3 and later are NOT affected; 'through 1.2.3' includes 1.2.3; ranges include endpoints as stated. Parse versions numerically by component (1.10 > 1.9; 2.0.1 > 2.0). If the advisory lists explicit affected versions, include only if the installed version is covered. If a fixed/patched version is stated and the installed version is at or above it, exclude. IMPORTANT: many advisories describe vulnerabilities in terms of version ranges, branches, or 'all versions prior to X' — evaluate these literally, and do not assume the installed version is safe without checking. If the advisory gives NO version information at all but the product is unambiguously installed, INCLUDE it. If the installed version cannot be determined for a product that is otherwise clearly installed, INCLUDE the advisory when the product match is unambiguous. When in genuine doubt about whether the version is covered, lean toward inclusion.

4. DO NOT USE OUTSIDE KNOWLEDGE TO ADD OR REMOVE IDs. Base every decision entirely on the supplied advisory text and supplied system profile. Never invent CVE IDs not in the list. Never exclude a genuinely matching advisory because you believe it is disputed, not exploitable, low severity, already mitigated, or because you recall a different affected range from memory — if the advisory's own affected data covers the installed product and version, it is applicable.

5. RECALL IS THE TOP PRIORITY — BE THOROUGH. Process EVERY advisory in the list, one at a time, including the last ones and those with long technical descriptions. Common failure modes to avoid: (a) missing a match because the advisory names the product differently from the profile (check abbreviations, vendor prefixes, ecosystem package names); (b) missing a match where the affected version is a RANGE rather than an explicit list — always evaluate the range against the installed version; (c) missing advisories for sub-components, libraries, or bundled dependencies present in the profile — check every indexed nested component against every advisory; (d) missing matches where the advisory affects an older or parallel branch of a product family and the installed version is in that branch; (e) missing matches where the product appears only in the advisory's prose description while the affected field is terse, or vice versa — read BOTH the description and the affected information for product and version cues; (f) missing an applicable advisory because its description is long or mostly about technical exploit details — scan the entire text for product/version mentions. When the advisory's affected information reasonably covers the installed version, include it rather than guessing it is out of scope.

6. AVOID FALSE POSITIVES. Do not include an advisory merely because its description mentions a product name in the inventory — the version must also be covered, or the advisory must lack version constraints. Do not include advisories for similar-sounding products from different vendors or different products sharing a substring. When the product identity is genuinely ambiguous (e.g., unclear which of two distinct products is meant), exclude; but when identity is clear and only version coverage is uncertain, include.

7. SYSTEMATIC PASS. Work through the advisories in order. For each: (a) identify every affected product named in the advisory (description AND affected fields); (b) find each in your profile index under any equivalent name, including nested dependencies; (c) if found, compare versions using the advisory's own semantics, defaulting to inclusion when version data is absent or the installed version is unknown; (d) record include/exclude. Do not skip advisories because they look low-severity, irrelevant, or duplicative of others — each ID needs its own decision. Before finalizing, do a second pass over any advisory you excluded solely on version grounds and re-verify the range semantics against the exact installed version string.

8. OUTPUT FORMAT. Return ONLY a JSON object of the exact form: {"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]} where the array contains the IDs of applicable advisories, each appearing at most once, drawn exclusively from the supplied advisories. Order does not matter. If none apply, return {"applicable_cves":[]}. Do not include any explanation, commentary, markdown, or text other than the JSON object.

Before finalizing, re-check: (a) every returned ID appears in the supplied advisories; (b) no ID is duplicated; (c) every returned advisory matches an installed product (including bundled/nested components) AND its version falls within the affected range or the advisory lacks version constraints; (d) you considered every advisory at least once, especially sub-component matches and advisories near the end of the list; (e) you did not exclude anything due to outside beliefs about exploitability, severity, or vendor disputes.","feedback":{"error_counts":{"invalid_output":0,"missed_applicable":41,"transport_failure":0,"unrelated_product":17,"version_excluded":49},"metrics":{"coverage":1.0,"failure_aware_lower_bound":{"fn":41,"fp":66,"micro_f1":0.3006535947712418,"precision":0.25842696629213485,"recall":0.359375,"tp":23},"scheduled":24,"valid":24,"valid_answers":{"fn":41,"fp":66,"micro_f1":0.3006535947712418,"precision":0.25842696629213485,"recall":0.359375,"tp":23}}},"feedback_version":"relational-abstractions-v2","task":"Write an instruction for matching a system inventory to a supplied list of CVE advisories. Input is JSON containing system_profile and advisories. Each advisory supplies its ID, description, and affected information. The answer must be a JSON object whose applicable_cves array contains unique IDs from that supplied list. Return your instruction as a JSON object with one nonempty prompt string of at most 8000 characters.","tier":1}
